# Overview of alcohol use

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Toxic and metabolic disorders > Overview of alcohol use*

[Original Article Link](/library/KP0UfT)

---

## Summary

<u>Unhealthy alcohol use</u> is any level of <u>alcohol</u> use associated with potential or actual harm and affects approximately 1 in 4 Americans. <u>Unhealthy alcohol use</u> can result in <u>acute alcohol intoxication</u>, <u>alcohol use disorder</u> (<u>AUD</u>), and <u>alcohol withdrawal</u>, as well as <u>complications of alcohol use</u> that include an increased risk of <u>chronic liver disease</u>, cancers, <u>heart</u> disease, injury, and premature <u>death</u>. All adults should be screened at least annually for <u>unhealthy alcohol use</u>; those with a positive screening should be evaluated for <u>complications of alcohol use</u> and offered assistance to reduce <u>alcohol</u> intake. The <u>SBIRT approach</u> (<u>screening, brief intervention, and referral to treatment</u>) is used to guide management. Patients with evidence of <u>AUD</u> or complicating comorbidities should be referred for specialist treatment. All other patients should be offered a <u>brief intervention for alcohol cessation</u>. <u>Unhealthy alcohol use</u> is often a chronic condition that requires long-term management.




Common <u>complications of alcohol use</u> are covered in “<u>Alcohol intoxication</u>,” “<u>Alcohol use disorder</u>,” “<u>Alcohol withdrawal</u>,” and “<u>Alcohol-associated liver disease</u>.”

---

## Evaluation of alcohol use

* Routinely screen all adults for early identification and <u>management of unhealthy alcohol use</u>.

* <u>Diagnostic studies to confirm alcohol use</u> are not usually required.

* Assess all patients with a positive screening for <u>complications of alcohol use</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Screening is necessary in all adults because <u>unhealthy alcohol use</u> is often overlooked; in two-thirds of cases of <u>unhealthy alcohol use</u> detected on screening, doctors had previously assumed <u>light to moderate alcohol use</u>. [[13]](/library/eIWxb50)

---

## Screening

### Indications [[1]](/library/BwczOe0)




* Adults aged ≥ 18 years: Consider at annual visits.  [[11]](/library/dIWob50)[[14]](/library/KIWUd50)[[15]](/library/THW6p50)

* Individuals aged < 18 years: See “<u>Adolescent health</u>.”

* Pregnant individuals: during the <u>first trimester</u> (see “<u>Prenatal care</u>”)

* More frequent screening may be indicated based on clinical judgment (e.g., patients with psychosocial issues) or chronic conditions (medical or psychiatric) that may be exacerbated by <u>alcohol</u> use. [[11]](/library/dIWob50)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Screening for unhealthy alcohol use</u> is underutilized: Only 1 in 6 adults in the US have ever been asked about their <u>alcohol</u> consumption by a <u>health care professional</u>. [[16]](/library/CDcqge0)




### Approach [[13]](/library/eIWxb50)[[14]](/library/KIWUd50)[[15]](/library/THW6p50)




* <u>Alcohol</u> use of any amount is considered positive screening for individuals who: [[17]](/library/6IWjd50)

* Are pregnant or may become pregnant

* Use medications that can lead to adverse effects if taken with <u>alcohol</u>

* Have medical or psychiatric conditions that are contraindications for <u>alcohol</u> use

* For all other patients: Use initial <u>screening tests</u> to identify <u>unhealthy alcohol use</u>.

* If initial <u>screening tests</u> are positive: Perform the <u>AUDIT questionnaire</u> to screen for <u>AUD</u>.





### Initial <u>screening tests</u>




#### Preferred <u>screening tests</u> [[1]](/library/BwczOe0)




The following tests can be used to assess for all forms of <u>unhealthy alcohol use</u>.




* Single alcohol screening question (<u>SASQ</u>):

* “Within the past 12 months, how many times have you had ≥ 5 drinks (for men ≤ 65 years) or ≥ 4 drinks (for women; men > 65 years) in a day?” [[1]](/library/BwczOe0)

* A positive screen is on ≥ 1 occasion.

* AUDIT-C test : 3-item questionnaire  [[1]](/library/BwczOe0)[[18]](/library/LIWwW50)





| <br><u>AUDIT-C</u> questionnaire [[19]](/library/ItWYUM0)<br> |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Questions | Score |  |  |  |  |
| 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |  |
| How often do you have an alcoholic drink? | Never | Once a month or less often | <br>2–4/month | <br>2–3/week | <br>≥ 4/week |
| How many alcoholic drinks do you have on an average day? | 1–2 | 3–4 | 5–6 | 7–9 | > 10 |
| How often do you have ≥ 6 alcoholic drinks on one occasion? | Never | Less than once a month | Monthly | Weekly | Daily <br> |
| <br>Positive score: ≥ 4 in men or ≥ 3 in women<br> |  |  |  |  |  |





![Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test-Concise (AUDIT-C)](media/rzwgxqne1xy4qpmdivr1k9s5.jpg)

Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test-Concise (AUDIT-C)




#### Alternative <u>screening tests</u>




The following tests are sometimes used as an initial screen for <u>AUD</u>, but cannot help to detect other forms of <u>unhealthy alcohol use</u>. [[1]](/library/BwczOe0)




##### CAGE questionnaire [[1]](/library/BwczOe0)




* 4-item questionnaire 

* Cut down drinking: Have you ever felt you should cut down on your drinking?

* Annoyed: Have people annoyed you by criticizing your drinking?

* Guilty: Have you ever felt guilty about drinking?

* Eye-opener: Have you ever felt you needed a drink first thing in the morning (<u>eye</u>-opener) to steady your nerves or to overcome a hangover?

* ≥ 2 affirmative answers: Screen for <u>alcohol use disorder</u> (e.g., with <u>AUDIT</u>).  [[13]](/library/eIWxb50)





##### Abbreviated forms of the Michigan <u>alcohol</u> <u>screening test</u> (MAST)




* Versions: brief MAST, short MAST (SMAST), and SMAST-geriatric  [[20]](/library/vtWA2M0)[[21]](/library/EtW82M0)

* Does not quantify <u>alcohol</u> use and can therefore miss <u>heavy drinking</u> [[22]](/library/HtWKUM0)





![Short Michigan Alcoholism Screening Test: Geriatric Version](media/sfagc7n624klpl8qefldojbw.jpg)

Short Michigan Alcoholism Screening Test: Geriatric Version




### AUDIT questionnaire [[1]](/library/BwczOe0)[[17]](/library/6IWjd50)[[18]](/library/LIWwW50)




* Typically performed if <u>SASQ</u> or <u>AUDIT-C test</u> are positive

* 10-item questionnaire; scored from 0–40 [[23]](/library/B8WzKM0)[[24]](/library/x8WEKM0)

* Scores of ≥ 8: associated with hazardous and <u>harmful alcohol use</u>

* Score ≥ 15 suggests <u>AUD</u>; proceed to <u>diagnostics for AUD</u>.





![Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT)](media/m5snm5k3j4gzqtdx4uqimdrp.jpg)

Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT)

## Confirmation of alcohol use

### Indications [[13]](/library/eIWxb50)




* Ongoing monitoring of <u>unhealthy alcohol use</u>

* Confirmation of abstinence

* To help diagnose <u>AUD</u>

* Patients who are unable to self-report <u>alcohol</u> use (e.g., individuals with cognitive impairment)





### Confirmation of recent <u>alcohol</u> use [[11]](/library/dIWob50)[[13]](/library/eIWxb50)[[25]](/library/S6Wy4m0)




* <u>Blood alcohol level</u>

* Measured with a rapid test or laboratory study

* Testing window: ≤ 12 hours since the last alcoholic drink [[25]](/library/S6Wy4m0)

* Ethanol metabolite tests  [[26]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Fatty acid ethyl esters

* Sample collection: multiple tissue types, usually blood or <u>hair</u>

* Testing window: typically ≤ 24 hours since the last alcoholic drink, but <u>alcohol</u> may be present for up to 8 days [[25]](/library/S6Wy4m0)[[27]](/library/Y11n2f0)

* Ethyl glucuronide or ethyl sulfate [[25]](/library/S6Wy4m0)

* Sample collection: typically urine

* Testing window: ≤ 5 days since the last alcoholic drink

* <u>False positives</u> are possible with renal impairment, <u>UTIs</u>, or exposure to low levels of <u>alcohol</u> in foods or products.  [[27]](/library/Y11n2f0)





### Confirmation of regular <u>heavy alcohol use</u>  [[13]](/library/eIWxb50)[[25]](/library/S6Wy4m0)




* Phosphatidylethanol (<u>PEth</u>): a collection of phospholipids that are formed following exposure to <u>alcohol</u> [[25]](/library/S6Wy4m0)

* The <u>half-life</u> of <u>PEth</u> correlates to the amount and frequency of <u>alcohol</u> intake.

* Can be detected for up to 28 days since the last drink in individuals with regular <u>heavy alcohol use</u>

* Cannot detect an isolated episode of <u>alcohol</u> use, only regular use or frequent <u>binge drinking</u>

* <u>Accuracy</u> is reduced if patients have received a <u>blood transfusion</u>.

* <u>Hair</u> <u>ethyl glucuronide</u>: detects <u>alcohol</u> use in the previous 3 months  [[25]](/library/S6Wy4m0)

* Carbohydrate-deficient transferrin: formed when <u>alcohol</u> inhibits <u>transferrin</u> <u>glycosylation</u> [[25]](/library/S6Wy4m0)

* Can detect regular <u>heavy alcohol use</u> in the previous 2–3 weeks

* Affected by <u>chronic liver disease</u>, <u>BMI</u>, <u>gender</u>, and <u>iron</u> disorders

* Markers of <u>end-organ dysfunction</u> [[25]](/library/S6Wy4m0)

* Can help in combination with other tests but lack <u>sensitivity</u> and <u>specificity</u>

* Examples include abnormal <u>liver chemistries</u> (e.g., elevated <u>GGT</u>) and elevated <u>MCV</u>.

---

## Assessment for complications of unhealthy alcohol use

<u>Alcohol</u> use can affect almost all systems of the body; see “<u>Complications of alcohol use</u>.”




### Clinical evaluation [[11]](/library/dIWob50)[[13]](/library/eIWxb50)




#### History




Perform a detailed <u>review of systems</u> and obtain collateral history (e.g., from family members and caregivers) when appropriate.




* Psychosocial history [[27]](/library/Y11n2f0)

* Current stressors (e.g., family, work)

* Mood or other psychiatric symptoms (e.g., <u>anxiety</u>, <u>depression</u>) [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* <u>Suicidality</u>

* Aggressive behaviors

* Current and past substance use

* <u>Tobacco smoking</u>

* Medication or substance misuse (e.g., <u>opioid use disorder</u>)  [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* Physical symptoms

* General (e.g., abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>nausea</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>, <u>headaches</u>) [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* <u>Sleep</u> disturbance [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* <u>Sexual dysfunction</u>

* <u>Menstrual cycle abnormalities</u> [[26]](/library/AN1Rdh0)





> [!TIP]
> Consider reviewing the state's <u>prescription drug monitoring program</u> to evaluate for unreported use of medications. [[11]](/library/dIWob50)




#### <u>Physical examination</u>




* Perform a comprehensive <u>physical examination</u> to assess for <u>alcohol-related complications</u>.

* If abnormalities are identified, order the appropriate studies.





### Diagnostic studies for alcohol-related complications




Based on clinical suspicion, order the appropriate studies for <u>alcohol-related complications</u>. [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)




#### <u>Laboratory studies</u>




The following findings are more common in patients with regular <u>heavy alcohol use</u>.




* <u>CBC</u>  [[11]](/library/dIWob50)[[26]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>Macrocytic anemia</u> (↓ <u>Hb</u>, ↑ <u>MCV</u>)

* ↓ <u>Platelets</u>  [[26]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>Iron deficient anemia</u> (↓ <u>iron</u>, ↑ <u>TIBC</u>, ↓ <u>ferritin</u>)

* <u>Anemia of chronic disease</u> (↓ <u>iron</u>, ↓ <u>TIBC</u>, ↑ <u>ferritin</u>)

* <u>Liver chemistries</u>

* ↑ <u>GGT</u>

* ↑ <u>ALT</u> and ↑ <u>AST</u>;  (<u>AST</u> > <u>ALT</u>) [[29]](/library/qIWCd50)

* See also “<u>Alcohol-associated liver disease</u>.”

* <u>BMP</u> and <u>electrolytes</u>

* ↓ <u>Creatinine</u> [[13]](/library/eIWxb50)

* ↓ Or ↑ <u>glucose</u>  [[26]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* ↑ <u>Lipase</u>, ↑ <u>amylase</u>  [[26]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* ↓ <u>Sodium</u>, ↓ <u>potassium</u>, ↓ <u>magnesium</u>, ↓ <u>phosphate</u>, ↓ <u>calcium</u>  [[26]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* <u>Vitamin</u> levels

* <u>B vitamins</u>: ↓ <u>vitamin B<sub>1</sub></u> (<u>thiamine</u>), ↓ <u>vitamin B<sub>6</sub></u> (<u>pyridoxine</u>), ↓ <u>vitamin B<sub>12</sub></u> (<u>cobalamin</u>)  [[11]](/library/dIWob50)[[26]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* ↓ <u>Folate</u>

* ↓ <u>Vitamin D</u>

* ↓ <u>Vitamin K</u>

* <u>Coagulation panel</u>: prolonged <u>PT</u>/<u>INR</u>  [[26]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[30]](/library/TnX6sA)

* Lipid levels: ↑ <u>triglycerides</u> [[26]](/library/AN1Rdh0)





#### Additional testing




Additional testing is performed based on clinical features.




* Cardiac symptoms : <u>ECG</u> and <u>echocardiography</u> [[26]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* Abnormal neurological findings: <u>neuroimaging</u> [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* <u>Symptoms of alcohol-associated hepatitis</u>, <u>symptoms of cirrhosis</u>, or diagnosis of <u>AUD</u>: <u>liver</u> <u>ultrasound</u> [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)[[31]](/library/Rlbl9F)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Heavy alcohol use</u> may have an impact on recommendations or frequency of screening programs, e.g., <u>screening for osteoporosis</u>. [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)[[32]](/library/uHXpHz)

---

## Management of unhealthy alcohol use

The <u>SBIRT approach</u> is used to guide management.




### Approach




* Manage any acute <u>alcohol-related complications</u> before further management steps; see:

* “<u>Management of alcohol intoxication</u>”

* “<u>Management of alcohol withdrawal</u>”

* “<u>Management of Wernicke encephalopathy</u>”

* Further management depends on drinking behavior and the desire to change.

* Patients who want to change <u>alcohol</u> use

* Evidence of <u>AUD</u> or complicating comorbidities, e.g., mental health conditions: Refer for treatment (see “<u>Management of AUD</u>”).

* <u>Unhealthy alcohol use</u> but no evidence of <u>AUD</u>: Offer a brief intervention. [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* Patient who do not want to change <u>alcohol</u> use

* Advise patients that they can return at any point to discuss <u>alcohol</u> use.

* Regularly review patients for <u>complications of alcohol use</u>.

* Discuss harm-reduction strategies with all patients.

* Identify and treat any medical <u>complications of alcohol use</u>; referral to a specialist may be required.

* Arrange follow-up and advise patients they can return at any point prior to that to discuss <u>alcohol</u> use.





> [!TIP]
> For patients who are abstinent or drink within the recommended guidelines, offer <u>positive reinforcement</u> and reiterate the guidelines for healthy <u>alcohol</u> use and when complete abstinence is recommended (e.g., during <u>pregnancy</u>). [[17]](/library/6IWjd50)




### Brief intervention for alcohol use [[14]](/library/KIWUd50)[[28]](/library/JIWsd50)




* Discussion of risk based on patient's screening results.

* Provide brief counseling (e.g., using <u>motivational interviewing</u> or the <u>5 As model of behavior change</u>).

* Educate on the <u>standard drink</u> and <u>low risk alcohol use</u>. [[5]](/library/-QWDAO0)

* Use <u>shared decision-making</u> to agree goals, e.g.: [[11]](/library/dIWob50)

* Abstinence

* Decrease <u>alcohol</u> consumption to recommended amount (e.g., <u>light to moderate alcohol use</u>) [[7]](/library/2mWTUN0)

* No <u>alcohol</u> use in situations that may cause harm to themselves or others (e.g., drinking before driving)

* Fewer drinking days [[17]](/library/6IWjd50)





> [!TIP]
> Advise full abstinence for those who are planning to conceive, taking medications that can cause harmful <u>drug interactions</u> (e.g., <u>metronidazole</u>), or have chronic comorbidities that may worsen <u>alcohol</u> use (e.g., <u>alcohol-associated liver disease</u>).




### Follow-up for <u>unhealthy alcohol use</u> [[14]](/library/KIWUd50)[[28]](/library/JIWsd50)




* Follow-up should be tailored to the patient's physical and mental health needs.

* Consider follow-up within 24 hours–1 week for patients starting <u>treatment for AUD</u> or at risk for <u>alcohol withdrawal</u>. [[14]](/library/KIWUd50)[[26]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* Schedule a follow-up visit in 1–3 months for patients who have undergone a brief intervention. [[17]](/library/6IWjd50)

* At the follow-up visit:

* Discuss progress toward goals.  [[14]](/library/KIWUd50)

* Modify treatment plans as needed. [[14]](/library/KIWUd50)

* Consider monitoring <u>CDT</u> or <u>GGT</u> levels for <u>positive reinforcement</u>.  [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* If needed, repeat monitoring for <u>complications of alcohol use</u>.

* For patients who have relapsed, shorten intervals between repeat follow-ups. [[14]](/library/KIWUd50)

* Patients usually require long-term monitoring and treatment because <u>unhealthy alcohol use</u> is often a chronic condition.





> [!TIP]
> Relapse is extremely common among patients with <u>unhealthy alcohol use</u>; discuss triggers for relapse and encourage patients to view relapses as <u>learning</u> opportunities rather than failures. [[14]](/library/KIWUd50)

## Complications of alcohol use

### Cardiac complications




* <u>Alcohol-induced atrial arrhythmia</u>

* <u>Ischemic heart disease</u> [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* <u>Hypertension</u> [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)





#### Alcohol-induced cardiomyopathy [[33]](/library/lVWvu40)[[34]](/library/hQXcDB)




* Definition: acquired <u>dilated cardiomyopathy</u> following regular <u>heavy alcohol use</u>

* Clinical features: <u>symptoms of heart failure</u>

* Diagnosis

* History of regular <u>heavy alcohol use</u>

* <u>Echocardiography</u>

* Dilation and impaired contractility of one or both ventricles

* Normal or reduced thickness of ventricular walls

* Systolic and <u>diastolic dysfunction</u>

* Exclusion of other possible causes of <u>dilated cardiomyopathy</u> (e.g., <u>coronary angiography</u> to rule out <u>coronary artery disease</u>)

* Management

* Total abstinence from <u>alcohol</u>

* <u>Treatment of heart failure</u>

* <u>Thiamine</u> and <u>folate supplementation</u>

* Prognosis: Ventricular function typically improves and may normalize with abstinence.





### Gastroenterological complications




* <u>Erosive gastritis</u>

* <u>Pancreatitis</u>

* <u>Alcohol-associated liver disease</u> (e.g., <u>steatosis</u>, <u>hepatitis</u>, <u>fibrosis</u>) [[35]](/library/y4ddNJ0)

* <u>Cirrhosis</u>





### Neuropsychiatric complications




* <u>Stroke</u> (hemorrhagic and <u>ischemic</u>) [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* <u>Meningitis</u>

* Mood disturbances: <u>anxiety</u>, <u>depression</u>, irritability, aggression  [[36]](/library/DGW1YM0)

* <u>Alcoholic hallucinations</u> [[26]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[27]](/library/Y11n2f0)

* <u>Insomnia</u> [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* <u>Polyneuropathy</u> [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* <u>Central pontine myelinolysis</u>





#### Alcohol-related cerebellar degeneration




* Definition: degeneration of Purkinje cells in the <u>cerebellar vermis</u> due to regular <u>heavy alcohol use</u>

* Clinical features

* <u>Gait ataxia</u>

* <u>Truncal ataxia</u>

* <u>Gaze-evoked nystagmus</u>

* Diagnostics: CT or <u>MRI</u> shows <u>atrophy</u> of the <u>cerebellar vermis</u>.





### Marchiafava–Bignami disease




* Definition: degeneration and <u>necrosis</u> of the corpus callosum, almost exclusively as a result of <u>malnutrition</u> due to regular <u>alcohol</u> use

* Clinical features

* Behavioral changes

* Cognitive impairment and <u>dementia</u>

* <u>Epileptic seizures</u>





### Multisystem complications




* <u>Cytochrome P450 induction</u>

* Increased risk of <u>malignancy</u>, e.g.: [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* <u>Liver cancer</u>

* <u>Breast cancer</u>

* <u>Colorectal cancer</u>

* <u>Head and neck cancers</u>

* <u>Esophageal cancer</u>

* <u>Vitamin deficiency</u>

* <u>Vitamin B<sub>1</sub> deficiency</u> (<u>thiamine deficiency</u>): <u>Wernicke-Korsakoff</u> syndrome

* <u>Vitamin B<sub>6</sub> deficiency</u>: <u>peripheral neuropathy</u>

* <u>Vitamin B<sub>9</sub> deficiency</u> (<u>folate deficiency</u>): <u>megaloblastic anemia</u>

* <u>Vitamin B<sub>12</sub> deficiency</u>: <u>subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord</u> (<u>funicular myelosis</u>), <u>megaloblastic anemia</u>

* <u>Alcohol-induced coagulopathy</u>

* <u>Electrolyte</u> abnormalities (see “<u>Evaluation for alcohol-related complications</u>”) [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* Hematological disorders including <u>anemia</u> (see “<u>Evaluation for alcohol-related complications</u>”) [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* <u>Zieve syndrome</u> [[37]](/library/9GWNYM0)





### Reproductive complications




* <u>Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder</u>  [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* <u>Preterm birth</u> [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* Testicular <u>atrophy</u> and <u>gynecomastia</u> [[26]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[38]](/library/BCXz8Z0)





### Musculoskeletal complications [[39]](/library/kVWmu40)[[40]](/library/OVWIu40)




* <u>Gout</u>: As the level of <u>alcohol</u> intake increases, so does the risk of <u>gout</u>. [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* <u>Osteoporosis</u>: <u>Heavy alcohol use</u> affects <u>bone density</u> and increases the risk of falls. [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)

* <u>Osteonecrosis of the femoral head</u>: associated with <u>heavy alcohol use</u> [[28]](/library/JIWsd50)





#### Acute alcohol-induced myopathy




* Definition: acute muscle <u>pain</u>, <u>weakness</u>, and swelling following the consumption of large quantities of <u>alcohol</u> in a short period of time

* Clinical features

* Most commonly focal and asymmetric <u>pain</u> of the <u>proximal</u> muscles (mainly the <u>pelvic</u> and <u>shoulder girdles</u>)

* Can lead to <u>rhabdomyolysis</u> and, subsequently, <u>acute kidney injury</u> (<u>pigment nephropathy</u>)

* Treatment [[40]](/library/OVWIu40)

* Total abstinence from <u>alcohol</u>: symptoms usually resolve within days to weeks.

* Optimization of nutrition





#### Chronic alcohol-induced myopathy




* Definition: progressive <u>muscle weakness</u> manifesting over weeks to months in individuals with regular <u>excessive alcohol use</u>

* Clinical features

* Most commonly <u>weakness</u> of the <u>proximal</u> muscles

* Occasionally muscle <u>pain</u>, <u>atrophy</u>, twitching, and/or <u>myotonia</u>

* Treatment [[40]](/library/OVWIu40)

* Total abstinence from <u>alcohol</u>: symptoms usually resolve within 2 to 12 months.

* Optimization of nutrition





> [!TIP]
> In <u>acute alcohol-induced myopathy</u>, <u>rhabdomyolysis</u> and subsequent <u>myoglobin</u> release can lead to <u>acute kidney injury</u>.

---
